name: Turbinate reduction

card.summary: Surgery that shrinks enlarged inferior turbinates to improve nasal breathing; a functional procedure with many techniques and limited high-quality comparisons.
card.note: Mainly a breathing procedure, not a cosmetic one; some forum posters warn about empty nose syndrome after aggressive reduction.

quick.overview:
Turbinates are folds of tissue inside the nose that warm and humidify air. When the inferior turbinates are enlarged they can block airflow, and turbinate reduction is the surgical family of methods used to shrink them. It is often paired with septoplasty or rhinoplasty.

In looksmaxxing forums it comes up in breathing-focused threads, usually alongside jaw and palate expansion, where members disagree about whether reduction is the right fix and discuss fear of over-resection.
quick.mechanism: Techniques include removing tissue (turbinectomy), cautery by electric, laser or radiofrequency methods, cryotherapy, and submucosal resection, with or without moving the bone outward. A review counted at least 13 techniques used over 130 years.
quick.risks: Reviews describe a serious lack of well-designed comparative studies. The goal in the literature is to reduce symptoms while preserving turbinate function. Forum members cite empty nose syndrome as a concern; its status is debated among clinicians and it is not assessed in the sources reviewed here.

lead: Turbinate reduction is a group of surgical procedures that reduce the size of the inferior turbinates, the mucosa-covered structures on the side walls of the nasal cavity, to relieve nasal obstruction. It is often combined with septoplasty or rhinoplasty because enlargement can occur on the side opposite a deviated septum, described as compensatory hypertrophy.[1][2]

A review of techniques counted at least 13 methods over 130 years and reported a serious lack of qualified studies, with prospective randomised comparisons being extremely rare. Its authors stated that the purpose of surgery should be to reduce complaints while preserving turbinate function.[3] A later randomised trial of 382 patients compared six techniques over six years of follow-up.[4]
In looksmaxxing communities the procedure is discussed mostly as a breathing intervention and compared with maxillary expansion, with some members warning against aggressive reduction.[5]
infobox: Turbinectomy, cautery (electro, laser, radiofrequency), cryotherapy, submucosal resection

paras: Turbinate hypertrophy can contribute to persistent nasal obstruction, and a paper on nasal airway obstruction describes turbinates among its anatomic contributors.[6] Turbinates warm and humidify inspired air, and a review of the controversies notes that obstruction can persist after septorhinoplasty if turbinate hypertrophy is not addressed.[7] Allergic rhinitis, a common cause of turbinate swelling, is the subject of a clinical practice guideline.[8]

The Siena randomised trial grouped patients into turbinectomy, laser cautery, electrocautery, cryotherapy, submucosal resection, and submucosal resection with lateral displacement.[4] Other reports describe alternative reduction techniques considered safe by their authors.[9] Registered trials have compared partial resection with radiofrequency ablation, and studied reduction under local anaesthesia.[10][11]

Randomised studies from the 1990s examined compensatory inferior turbinate hypertrophy after septoplasty and evaluated turbinoplasty with acoustic rhinometry and long-term follow-up.[2][12] A study of the NOSE scale in septoplasty without turbinate reduction compared the scale with other measures.[13] Registered trials are examining septoplasty with and without turbinate reduction.[14][15]

Reviews emphasise preserving turbinate function when reducing tissue.[3] On looksmax.org, one poster told others to look up empty nose syndrome and avoid reduction, while another replied that reduction is the only fix for true turbinate obstruction.[5] The sources reviewed here do not contain a study of empty nose syndrome.
Opioid use after rhinoplasty has also been studied as part of peri-operative care.[16]

A 382-patient randomised trial compared six reduction techniques over six years.[4] Randomised studies examined turbinoplasty after septoplasty.[2][12] The review literature judges comparative evidence to be scarce.[3] Registered trials include a terminated phase 4 study of surgical reduction for obstruction, a completed trial of radiofrequency reduction in persistent allergic rhinitis, a 242-patient trial of turbinate reduction to improve CPAP outcomes in sleep apnoea, and a trial of reduction under local anaesthesia.[17][18][19][11]

timeline.event: Randomised study of compensatory turbinate hypertrophy after septoplasty using acoustic rhinometry.[2]
Long-term results after randomised turbinoplasty published.[12]
Review counts at least 13 surgical techniques over 130 years.[3]
Randomised trial of six techniques with six-year follow-up.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org turbinate reduction is mentioned in nasal-breathing threads, often compared with maxillary expansion.[5]

claims.claim: Turbinate reduction should be avoided at all costs because of empty nose syndrome.
claims.believers: One poster tells readers to search for empty nose syndrome and not to have a reduction.[5]
claims.experts: Reviews state that surgery should reduce symptoms while preserving turbinate function.[3] No study in the reviewed sources quantifies empty nose syndrome after reduction.

claims.claim: If turbinates are truly oversized, reduction is the only thing that fixes the blockage.
claims.believers: Another poster says reduction is the only fix for real turbinate blockage and calls alternatives such as maxillary expansion gimmick procedures.[5]
claims.experts: Randomised trials of reduction techniques exist, but a review called qualified comparative studies extremely rare.[3][4] Medical therapy for allergic rhinitis is covered in a clinical practice guideline.[8]
